document.abstract: The development of high-pressure discharge lamps over the years has been aimed at improving color rendering, efficiency and life. The compact-source iodide (CSI) lamp was initially developed in 400-W and 1,000-W ratings for projector applications, but it was the new demands of outside broadcast color television in 1969 that led to the introduction of this lamp housed in a PAR-64 sealed-beam globe for floodlighting sports stadia from high corner towers. Sports areas with sidelighting were not so well suited to the use of the symmetrical beam CSI floodlights, so another metal halide lamp was introduced — this one with an unjacketed linear arc tube — in 750-W and 1,600-W ratings. For filming, the 1-kW lamp performs exceptionally well as a fill-in source with daylight. At 90 lm/W, it is five to six times more efficient than tungsten-halogen lamps used with blue filters to correct the daylight; four lamps are approximately equivalent to a 225-A brute arc. Control gear is being made simpler and more versatile, and the problem of “beat,” which is already controllable in filming situations, is expected to be overcome completely with techniques now being developed.
